inputs.original_text: Harry Wait was found guilty of two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge after requesting ballots for Robin Vos and Cory Mason without their consent, though he was acquitted of another identity theft count. His claim that he was exposing vulnerabilities doesn’t excuse manufacturing fraud—but neither does this case justify making voting harder for ordinary people. The real danger is turning isolated misconduct into an excuse to undermine public trust or restrict access. We need election systems that are both secure and accessible, and accountability that protects voters rather than punishing them.
inputs.modified_text: Harry Wait was found guilty of two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge for requesting ballots for Robin Vos and Cory Mason without their consent; he was acquitted of another identity theft count. Calling it a test of election security doesn’t erase the harm of manufacturing fraud. But the answer cannot be to make voting harder for everyone—especially when access barriers fall hardest on people already underserved by the system. This should prompt stronger, fairer safeguards and accountability, not give anyone an excuse to erode public trust or restrict the right to vote.
